title: Look at Me
full_review:
Somehow Europeans have the knack of making keenly observant movies about the complexities of ordinary life beyond the ken of most Hollywood filmmakers.

Such a film is the affecting, character-driven "Look at Me" (Sony Classics) from France which centers on Lolita (Marilou Berry), the unhappy, overweight, 20-year-old daughter of Etienne Cassard (Jean-Pierre Bacri), an egocentric, celebrated writer. Lolita feels very much the ugly duckling, particularly in light of her father's pretty young girlfriend, Karine (Virginie Desarnauts).

Lolita has aspirations of becoming a classical singer, and her chief joys in life are her lessons and the amateur chorale of which she's a member. Otherwise, she lumbers placidly through life and seems to accept her wallflower lot. Much to her frustration, her father takes virtually no interest in his daughter's vocalizing, but is otherwise reasonably caring if utterly self-absorbed.

Lolita has a boyfriend of sorts, but we sense (correctly, as it happens) that her adoring feelings for him are not reciprocated. When Sebastien (Keine Bouhiza), a young stranger she selflessly covers with her coat when she sees him passed out on the sidewalk outside a club, asks to meet her to thank her for her compassion (and return the coat), she infuriatingly treats him with only tolerant civility, even though it's plain to see he's an exceptionally nice fellow.

Lolita's singing teacher, Sylvia (director and co-writer Agnes Jaoui), has reluctantly agreed to tutor her amateur group. Later, she decides to renege on her promise, but changes her tune when she learns the identity of Lolita's father, whose writing she admires. She also believes that getting to know Etienne through his daughter will help her novelist husband, Pierre (Laurent Grevill), currently in a serious creative funk, advance his career.

Jaoui's perceptive film -- co-written with Bacri -- says much about youthful angst, fathers and daughters, celebrities and the sycophants who surround them, all in a marvelously real way. The brilliant opening sequence in a taxicab, contrasting how Lolita lets a surly driver walk all over her, while Etienne, when he later gets in the car, puts the driver soundly in his place, is the kind of inconsequential episode that gives us immediate insight into the characters.

The acting is superb all around. Berry is just perfect: lumpish but kind, occasionally unsympathetic, and transformed when she "sings." (Her singing was dubbed by Alexandra Rubner.) Bacri is utterly plausible as the autocratic literary lion. The versatile Jaoui telegraphs a genuine caring quality but not without a degree of self-interest. Grevill, Bouhiza and Desarnauts all satisfyingly inhabit their characters, while Gregoire Oestermann and Michele Moretti are especially good as Etienne's lackey and Pierre's agent, respectively.

If the feel-good ending is rather conventional, the film rarely makes a false move.

Like that other Gallic hit, "Les Choristes," music -- here, ranging from the chorale's Baroque tunes to Mozart's "Cosi Fan Tutte" -- is used quite effectively throughout, providing texture to Lolita's character and serving as lovely underscoring for its own sake.

The film, with subtitles, contains a few instances of rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
